sections.p17.s0: Concepts for moving data reliably. Read items 0 to 5 first, since they set the vocabulary, then take 6 to 11 alongside the build. Run a small example for each item in DuckDB or Python rather than only reading. About 40 per cent of the phase.
sections.p17.s1: Build one pipeline from a public API into DuckDB that runs on a schedule without you. Work in order: raw landing, transform, load, tests, orchestration, then backfill, lineage and the Polars swap. Leave it running for a week before you call it done.

p17.s0.0.how: Read the Kafka introduction and the batch and stream processing chapters of Designing Data-Intensive Applications. For five cases (daily sales report, fraud check at checkout, hourly dashboard, search index update, monthly billing), write the latency needed and choose batch, micro-batch or streaming.
p17.s0.0.done: You can justify each choice from the required latency and explain why streaming costs more to run and debug.

p17.s0.1.how: Read dbt's article on ETL versus ELT. Do the same transform twice: once in Python before loading into DuckDB, and once by loading the raw data and transforming it with SQL inside DuckDB. Note what you can rebuild later in each case.
p17.s0.1.done: You can explain how cheap warehouse compute and keeping raw data made ELT the default, and when ETL is still required.

p17.s0.2.how: Read Airflow's best practices on idempotent tasks. Write a daily load that deletes and rewrites the rows for its run date inside one transaction, or upserts on a key with INSERT OR REPLACE. Run it three times for the same date and compare counts and totals.
p17.s0.2.done: Three runs for the same date leave identical row counts and totals, checked by a query.

p17.s0.3.how: Read Airflow's DAG run page on catchup and backfill. Load a day, then add records for that day with an older event time, and write a rule for reprocessing by event date with a lookback window of N days. Apply the rule and check the late rows arrive.
p17.s0.3.done: You can explain event time versus processing time, and your pipeline picks up late records that fall inside its lookback window.

p17.s0.4.how: Write the same 10-million-row table to CSV and to Parquet partitioned by date with DuckDB COPY tbl TO 'out' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (dt)). Compare total size and the run time of a one-day filtered query on each.
p17.s0.4.done: You have measured size and query-time figures for both formats and can explain column pruning and partition pruning.

p17.s0.5.how: Read the introduction of the CIDR 2021 Lakehouse paper. Write one paragraph each on a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse covering where the data sits, who enforces the schema, and how updates are made atomic. Note the role of table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg.

where.name: Databricks: What is a data lakehouse?

p17.s0.5.done: You can explain the three in two minutes and say which one DuckDB over a folder of Parquet files resembles.

p17.s0.6.how: Read dbt's page on model contracts. In a source table, add a column, rename a column and change a type, and see which downstream queries break or silently change. Then add a contract to one model so a breaking change fails the build.
p17.s0.6.done: You can say which changes are backward compatible, and a renamed column now fails your build instead of producing nulls.

p17.s0.7.how: Write not_null, unique, accepted_values and relationships tests in dbt, or the same checks with pandera or plain SQL, plus a value-range check. Insert one bad row per check on purpose and run the tests.
p17.s0.7.done: Each of the five checks fails on its planted row and passes on clean data.

p17.s0.8.how: Build a dbt incremental model using is_incremental() and a unique_key, or the same logic in SQL with a high-water mark on an updated-at column. Then read the Debezium overview to see how change data capture reads the database log instead of polling.
p17.s0.8.done: A rerun processes only new or changed rows, shown by row counts, and you can explain why log-based CDC sees deletes and polling does not.

p17.s0.9.how: Read Airflow's pages on DAGs and tasks. Write a DAG with three dependent tasks, set retries and retry_delay, add an on_failure_callback that posts to a webhook or writes a file, and add a check that alerts if the run has not finished by a set time. Make one task fail.
p17.s0.9.done: The failing task retries the configured number of times and then fires the alert, visible in the UI or the log.

p17.s0.10.how: Run Kafka locally from the quickstart, create a topic with 3 partitions, and produce keyed messages. Start two consumers in one group, stop one to watch the partitions rebalance, and read committed offsets with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe.
p17.s0.10.done: You can explain why order holds only within a partition and what is lost if offsets are committed before processing.

p17.s0.11.how: Read BigQuery's cost-control best practices. In DuckDB, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a query over partitioned Parquet with and without a partition filter, and with SELECT * versus two columns. Compare rows scanned and run time.
p17.s0.11.done: You can estimate how much data a query will scan before running it and show a filter cutting that by an order of magnitude.

p17.s1.0.how: Choose a public API with daily data, such as weather or transport. Write a script that fetches one day with httpx, handles paging and rate limits, and writes the untouched JSON to raw/source=name/date=YYYY-MM-DD/ with a fetch timestamp.
p17.s1.0.done: Each run writes one raw file per date, and rerunning a date replaces its file rather than adding a second one.

p17.s1.1.how: Set up dbt with the dbt-duckdb adapter. Write staging models that parse and type the raw JSON, then mart models for the questions you want answered, and add tests to every staging model.
p17.s1.1.done: dbt build runs every model and test from raw to marts with no failures.

p17.s1.2.how: Write the mart tables to a DuckDB file and export the main fact table as Parquet partitioned by date. Make each load replace only the partitions for the dates in that run.
p17.s1.2.done: Loading one date changes only that date's partition, confirmed by per-date row counts before and after.

p17.s1.3.how: Keep test severity at error, the dbt default, and make the orchestrator task fail on a non-zero exit from dbt build. Add source freshness and row-count checks, plant a duplicate key, and confirm the run stops before the marts are built.
p17.s1.3.done: A planted bad row turns the scheduled run red and no downstream task runs.

p17.s1.4.how: Wrap ingest, transform, test and load as tasks in an Airflow DAG or a Prefect flow on a daily schedule. Give the ingest task retries with a delay, send an alert on failure, and run it under the scheduler, not by hand.
p17.s1.4.done: The pipeline runs daily for a week without you, and a forced API failure retries and then alerts.

p17.s1.5.how: Add a backfill --start --end command that loops over dates and runs the same idempotent per-date task, or use your orchestrator's backfill feature. Run it for a past month, run it again, and compare per-day totals.
p17.s1.5.done: A month backfills with one command, and the second run leaves every per-day row count unchanged.

p17.s1.6.how: Add descriptions for every model and column in the dbt YAML files, run dbt docs generate and dbt docs serve, and check the lineage graph. Add a README section naming the source API, schedule, owner and each mart.
p17.s1.6.done: Someone new can find, from the docs alone, which source feeds a given mart column and when it refreshes.

p17.s1.7.how: Take the heaviest pandas step in the pipeline and rewrite it with the Polars lazy API: scan_parquet, filter, group_by, collect. Run both on the same data, measure time and peak memory, and compare outputs.
p17.s1.7.done: The outputs are equal row for row, and you have measured time and memory figures for both versions.
